title: Interactive problems (query–response, binary-search interactive)
relevance: Medium — almost never a literal OA template (no flush/interactor), but CF/AtCoder Div2 C–D interactives are common; the skill transfers to “limited oracle / ask ≤ Q questions” interview twists and to any BS-on-answer thinking under a query budget.
company_notes: Interview twists: broken version / first bad commit with ≤ log n asks (git-bisect / Hidden Integer style); hidden array with range-sum or second-max oracles to find max / k-th zero; recover secret perm/password via compares or mod under a budget; two sorted lists behind APIs — global k-th with few fetches.

phases.goal: Spot interactive / limited-oracle problems from protocol wording and a hard query budget.

must_hit.point: Recognize Interactive statements by “Interactive”, a `?`/`!` query–answer protocol, or “at most Q questions.”
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names those stems and says the judge holds a hidden object you probe with queries.

must_hit.point: The skill transfers to interview “limited oracle / ask ≤ Q questions” twists even when there is no flush/interactor OA template.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps OA-style ask-budget problems to the same interactive pattern.

must_hit.point: Classic disguise: find the broken version / first bad commit with ≤ log n asks (git-bisect style).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites first-bad / bisect as interactive binary search under a log-budget.

probes: What wording tells you this is interactive rather than offline I/O?
How does a “≤ Q questions” interview twist relate to CF interactive problems?

hints.1: Look for protocol tokens, not only for CF’s Interactive tag.
hints.2: Scan for Interactive / `?`–`!` / at most Q questions, and a hidden object.
hints.3: Say: Interactive or ask-budget wording → print queries, read answers, finish under Q (often ≈ log N).

phases.goal: Map the query limit to the right search/reconstruct strategy before designing queries.

must_hit.point: Map the query limit to an algorithm: ≈log → binary/ternary search; ≈N → one pass / degree queries; N log N → sort/merge with comparisons; bit-width → recover each bit (often in parallel).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that budget shape, not just “binary search,” chooses the method.

must_hit.point: Interactive BS keeps a feasible interval (or set) and asks a mid that halves remaining candidates given the oracle type (compare / count / second-max / distance).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes shrinking candidates with an oracle-aware mid, not a blind array mid.

must_hit.point: 2·⌈log⌉ budgets suggest independent searches on two axes (e.g. missing row and column separately).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Splits a 2D search into two independent log-budget searches.

probes: Given a query limit, how do you choose between binary search, linear reconstruct, and sorting with comparisons?
What does a good mid query do to the remaining candidate set?

hints.1: Read Q first—budget dictates the algorithm family.
hints.2: log → BS/ternary; ~N → linear/degree/cycles; N log N → comparator sort; bit-width → bits.
hints.3: Keep a feasible set; pick mid that halves it under the oracle (compare/count/second-max/distance); two axes may need two independent log searches.

phases.goal: Show flush I/O discipline and concrete interactive templates (BS, reconstruct, bit/XOR).

must_hit.point: Always flush after every query (`endl` / `fflush` / `sys.stdout.flush`); never read before the query is flushed; print the final `!` answer and exit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names flush + no-read-before-flush + terminate immediately after `!`.

must_hit.point: Second-max / argmax-on-range oracles: the max lies in the half that contains the global second-max’s side (Guessing the Greatest family).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses a range second-max answer to decide which half holds the maximum.

must_hit.point: Reconstruct permutations via comparator sort, `a%b` tricks (larger residue is larger), or following `p[i]` as a functional graph of cycles.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names at least one of those three reconstruct templates with the matching query type.

probes: Walk through the flush/`!` I/O rules you use on every interactive problem.
With a range second-max oracle, how do you decide which half contains the maximum?

hints.1: Interactive bugs are often I/O, not the search math.
hints.2: Flush every query; read only after flush; print `!` and stop.
hints.3: Template: flush mid-query → shrink by oracle; for second-max, keep the half on the second-max’s side; for perms use compares, `a%b`, or cycle-follow.

phases.goal: Treat the query limit as the complexity bound and match asks to information-theoretic cost.

must_hit.point: Query-limit is the complexity: ≈log ⇒ binary/ternary search; ≈n ⇒ linear reconstruct / degree / cycle-follow; ≈n log n ⇒ sorting with comparisons; ≈bitwidth ⇒ recover each bit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Equates allowed asks to the algorithm’s ask count, not wall-clock alone.

must_hit.point: Bit/XOR oracles pack information: chosen masks so each answer bit encodes one unknown, or two queries packing low/high halves.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes encoding many unknowns into few answers via masks or half-packing.

must_hit.point: Cycle-follow reconstruct of a hidden permutation can finish in ≤ n+1 asks; distance-from-root tree reconstruct can use O(n) asks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites ≤ n+1 cycle closes or O(n) distance queries as linear-budget reconstruct.

probes: How do you justify that your strategy fits under the stated ask limit?
When is recovering bit-by-bit cheaper than searching the full domain?

hints.1: Count asks the same way you’d count time complexity.
hints.2: Match ≈log / ≈n / ≈n log n / bitwidth to BS / linear / sort / bits.
hints.3: Say: budget ≈ that family; XOR/masks pack bits into few queries; cycles ≤ n+1 or tree distances O(n) when the limit is linear.

phases.goal: Catch flush mistakes, wrong budget mapping, and adaptive/lying interactors.

must_hit.point: Forgetting to flush (or reading before flush) so the judge never sees the query; buffered output is not enough without flush.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that missing flush hangs or wrong-answers interactive submissions.

must_hit.point: Failing to terminate immediately after printing `!`, or continuing to query after the answer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says print `!` then exit—no extra I/O.

must_hit.point: Lying / adaptive interactors: spend early queries to learn the lie schedule (Rocket) or keep the search range large enough versus expansion (Subway Pursuit).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Plans either learn-lies-then-BS or maintain slack against a growing interval.

probes: What is the most common way interactive solutions hang against the judge?
How do you adapt binary search when some answers may lie or the feasible range expands each turn?

hints.1: Think I/O and adaptive oracles, not only off-by-one.
hints.2: Flush every query; stop after `!`; for liars/expanders, learn the schedule or keep slack.
hints.3: Local interactor checking flush + query count; Rocket learn-lies then BS; Subway Pursuit keep range large enough vs expansion.

tradeoffs.topic: Binary/ternary search vs linear reconstruct vs comparator sort
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Choose by query budget: ≈log → binary/ternary search; ≈N → one pass / degree / cycle-follow; N log N → sort/merge with comparisons; bit-width → recover each bit, often in parallel.

tradeoffs.topic: Comparator sort vs mod queries vs cycle-follow for permutations
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use less-than queries when the limit is ≈n log n; `i%j`/`j%i` when residues reveal order (larger residue is larger); follow next-pointer queries when you can close cycles in ≤ n+1 asks.

tradeoffs.topic: Distance-from-root layers vs LCA-on-leaves prune for trees
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Distance queries from one node give layers/bipartition (Lost Tree); LCA queries on leaves prune toward the root (Kuroni)—pick the oracle the statement gives.

tradeoffs.topic: Independent two-axis search vs joint 2D search
tradeoffs.strong_answer: When the budget is about 2·⌈log⌉, run independent binary searches on each axis (e.g. missing row and column with rectangle counts) instead of one coupled 2D search.

gotchas.trap: Printing a query then reading immediately without flushing.
gotchas.correction: Always flush (`endl` / `fflush` / `sys.stdout.flush`) after every query; never read before the query is flushed.

gotchas.trap: Leaving the program running after printing the final `!` answer.
gotchas.correction: Print the final `!` answer and exit immediately.

gotchas.trap: Picking binary search when the query limit is linear or n log n-shaped.
gotchas.correction: Map limit → algorithm: ≈log BS/ternary; ≈n linear/degree/cycles; ≈n log n comparator sort; bit-width bit recovery.

gotchas.trap: Assuming buffered stdout reaches the judge without an explicit flush.
gotchas.correction: Local-test with an interactor that checks flush and query count; sync I/O off only if you still flush.

gotchas.trap: Treating a lying or expanding interactor like a normal monotone binary search.
gotchas.correction: Learn the lie schedule first (Rocket) or keep the search range large enough against expansion (Subway Pursuit).
